claim: Programmed cell death causes the loss of up to 50% of neurons in rodents during brain development.
source: Programmed cell death widely but heterogeneously affects the developing brain, causing the loss of up to 50% of neurons in rodents.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Nikolić et al., 2013; Dekkers et al., 2013; Southwell et al., 2012).

claim: The primary motor cortex (M1) and primary somatosensory cortex (S1) display striking differences in density of apoptotic neurons during the early postnatal period.
source: Here, we report that the primary motor cortex (M1) and primary somatosensory cortex (S1), two adjacent but functionally distinct areas, display striking differences in density of apoptotic neurons during the early postnatal period.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Differences in rate of apoptosis between M1 and S1 negatively correlate with region-dependent levels of activity.
source: These differences in rate of apoptosis negatively correlate with region-dependent levels of activity.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo recordings showing higher activity in S1 than M1 (Figure 4) and lower apoptosis in S1 than M1 (Figure 3).

claim: Disrupting electrical activity pharmacologically alters the spatial pattern of apoptosis.
source: Disrupting this activity either pharmacologically or by electrical stimulation alters the spatial pattern of apoptosis and sensory deprivation leads to exacerbated amounts of apoptotic neurons in the corresponding functional area of the neocortex.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments using 4-AP/0 Mg2+ and gabazine treatments (Figure 5) and kainate injections (Figure 7A).

claim: Sensory deprivation leads to exacerbated amounts of apoptotic neurons in the corresponding functional area of the neocortex.
source: Disrupting this activity either pharmacologically or by electrical stimulation alters the spatial pattern of apoptosis and sensory deprivation leads to exacerbated amounts of apoptotic neurons in the corresponding functional area of the neocortex.
evidence: This is demonstrated by whisker deafferentation experiments showing increased apoptosis in the corresponding barrel field (Figure 7B).

claim: A first wave of apoptosis peaks at embryonic day (E) 14 in the rodent cortex and is believed to select the appropriate neural clones.
source: A first wave of apoptosis, peaking at embryonic day (E) 14 in the rodent cortex, is believed to select the appropriate neural clones (Blaschke et al., 1996, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by Blaschke et al.

claim: A second surge of apoptosis affects the early postnatal cortex, triggering the loss of up to 50% of newly differentiated neurons.
source: A second surge of apoptosis affects the early postnatal cortex, triggering the loss of up to 50% of newly differentiated neurons (Nikolić et al., 2013; Dekkers et al., 2013; Southwell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The death of developing neurons is mediated by the evolutionary conserved mitochondrial pathway.
source: The death of developing neurons is mediated by the evolutionary conserved mitochondrial pathway (Shi, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shi, 2001.

claim: In the mammalian brain, the mitochondrial apoptosis pathway is highly regulated by proteins of the Bcl-2 family.
source: In the mammalian brain, this intracellular pathway is highly regulated by proteins of the Bcl-2 family (Southwell et al., 2012; Ledonne et al., 2016; Nakamura et al., 2016; Shindler et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: In the peripheral nervous system, neurotrophins represent the main pro-survival factors by activating the PI3K/Akt and Raf/MEK/ERK pathways, while inhibiting the JNK pathway.
source: In the peripheral nervous system, neurotrophins represent the main pro-survival factors by activating the PI3K/Akt and Raf/MEK/ERK pathways, while inhibiting the JNK pathway (Kristiansen and Ham, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kristiansen and Ham, 2014.

claim: The neurotrophic theory does not apply to the central nervous system.
source: However, experiments using transgenic mice have shown that this so-called 'neurotrophic theory' does not apply to the central nervous system (Jones et al., 1994; Minichiello and Klein, 1996; Dekkers et al., 2013; Silos-Santiago et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple transgenic mouse studies.

claim: In developing cortical neurons, the intracellular Akt/PI3K pathway is of particular importance to promote neuronal survival.
source: In developing cortical neurons, the intracellular Akt/PI3K pathway is of particular importance to promote neuronal survival (Wagner-Golbs and Luhmann, 2012; Golbs et al., 2011; Murase et al., 2011; Datta et al., 1997; Bittigau et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: An increase in spontaneous activity is commonly associated with a decreased rate of apoptosis.
source: In general, an increase in spontaneous activity is commonly associated with a decreased rate of apoptosis whereas a reduction of electrical activity exacerbates the number of central neurons undergoing apoptosis (Golbs et al., 2011; Murase et al., 2011; Ikonomidou et al., 1999; Lebedeva et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A reduction of electrical activity exacerbates the number of central neurons undergoing apoptosis.
source: In general, an increase in spontaneous activity is commonly associated with a decreased rate of apoptosis whereas a reduction of electrical activity exacerbates the number of central neurons undergoing apoptosis (Golbs et al., 2011; Murase et al., 2011; Ikonomidou et al., 1999; Lebedeva et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Transplantation studies with embryonic GABAergic interneuron populations suggest that both the extent and time point of cell death in cortical inhibitory neurons are intrinsically determined.
source: On the other hand, transplantation studies with embryonic GABAergic interneuron populations suggest that both the extent and time point of cell death in cortical inhibitory neurons are intrinsically determined (Southwell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Southwell et al., 2012.

claim: The overall rate of cell death in the developing mouse neocortex increases from P2 on, peaks around P5 to P6 and subsequently declines.
source: In agreement with previous reports (Southwell et al., 2012; Verney et al., 2000), the overall rate of cell death in the developing mouse neocortex increases from P2 on, peaks around P5 to P6 and subsequently declines (Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1; one-way ANOVA, R²=0.54, p=0.002, n = 38 mice).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and statistical analysis, as well as citations to previous reports.

claim: Cell death at P5-7 almost exclusively affects GFAP-negative, neuronal cells.
source: Cell death at this developmental stage almost exclusively affects GFAP-negative, neuronal cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The majority of aCasp3-positive neurons are GAD67-negative, glutamatergic neurons with a minor contribution of GAD67-positive, GABAergic neurons.
source: Consistent with previous work (Southwell et al., 2012; Sahara et al., 2012), the majority of aCasp3-positive neurons are GAD67-negative, glutamatergic neurons with a minor contribution of GAD67-positive, GABAergic neurons (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figures 1C and D, and citations to previous work.

claim: The primary motor cortex (M1) shows higher densities of aCasp3-positive cells (39.66 ± 14.93 aCasp3/mm²) compared to the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) (15.51 ± 6.90 aCasp3/mm²) in flat-mounted sections.
source: Most obviously, the primary motor cortex (M1) shows higher densities of aCasp3-positive cells (39.66 ± 14.93 aCasp3/mm²) compared to the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) (15.51 ± 6.90 aCasp3/mm²; n = 3 mice), although the difference is not significant (t-test, p=0.28).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of flat-mounted sections, though the difference is not statistically significant.

claim: In most cases, aCasp3-positive neurons are located in layer II at the border of layer I.
source: In most cases, aCasp3-positive neurons are located in layer II at the border of layer I (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 2C.

claim: aCasp3 labeling allows the detection of apoptotic neurons at various stages of morphological and nuclear degradation.
source: Note that aCasp3 labeling allows the detection of apoptotic neurons at various stages of morphological and nuclear degradation.
evidence: This is based on observations from the immunohistochemical analysis and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Superficial cortical layers (layers I-IV) show a higher rate of cell death (29.31 ± 4.13 aCasp3/mm²) compared to deeper layers (layer V: 18.73 ± 1.61 aCasp3/mm²; layer VI: 6.76 ± 0.85 aCasp3/mm²).
source: Quantification of the number of aCasp3-labeled neurons revealed a higher rate of cell death in superficial cortical layers (Figure 3A and Figure 3—source data 1; layers I-IV: 29.31 ± 4.13 aCasp3/mm²) compared to deeper layers (layer V: 18.73 ± 1.61 aCasp3/mm²; layer VI; 6.76 ± 0.85 aCasp3/mm²; two-way ANOVA layer p=0.0002; post-hoc test sector a p<0.001, sectors b to f p>0.05; n = 11 mice).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3A with statistical analysis.

claim: Cell death is four times higher in M1 (sectors a/b: 57.76 ± 10.26 aCasp3/mm²) than in S1 (sectors c-f: 14.86 ± 1.52 aCasp3/mm²).
source: Furthermore, cell death is four times higher in M1 (Figure 3A; sectors a/b: 57.76 ± 10.26 aCasp3/mm²) than in S1 (sectors c-f: 14.86 ± 1.52 aCasp3/mm²; t-test, p<0.0001)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3A with statistical analysis.

claim: In layer V, lower rates of cell death are detectable in M1 (sectors a/b: 13.79 ± 2.40 aCasp3/mm²) compared to S1 (sectors c-f: 29.97 ± 2.04 aCasp3/mm²).
source: In layer V, lower rates of cell death are detectable in M1 (sectors a/b: 13.79 ± 2.40 aCasp3/mm²) compared to S1 (sectors c-f: 29.97 ± 2.04 aCasp3/mm²; t-test, p=0.03).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis with statistical testing.

claim: The deeper layer VI displays a low amount of apoptotic neurons and does not exhibit any area specificity.
source: The deeper layer VI displays a low amount of apoptotic neurons and does not exhibit any area specificity (two-way ANOVA, sector p>0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of quantitative data.

claim: The spatial pattern of cell death at P5-7 detected by aCasp3 immunohistochemistry was confirmed by TUNEL staining.
source: The spatial pattern of cell death at P5-7 detected by aCasp3 immunohistochemistry was confirmed by TUNEL staining, which labels fragmented nuclei when cell death process is fully executed (Gavrieli et al., 1992). The pattern of TUNEL-positive neurons can be superimposed on the pattern of aCasp3-labeled neurons (Figure 3B and Figure 3—source data 2; two-way ANOVA, sector p<0.001, detection method p=0.96, n = 3 animals)
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 3B with statistical analysis, and a citation to the TUNEL method.

claim: In P1-3 and P9-11 mice, the density of apoptotic neurons is very low and does not reveal any sector differences.
source: In contrast to P5-7 mice, the density of apoptotic neurons detected in both P1-3 and P9-11 mice is very low and does not reveal any sector differences (two-way ANOVA, P1-3: sector p=0.48, n = 8 animals; P9-11: sector p=0.45, n = 9 animals).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis with statistical testing shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: In P9-11 mice, significantly higher amounts of cell death are detected in layer V than in more superficial layers.
source: But, whereas apoptosis similarly affects all layers in P1-3 mice (layer p=0.08), significantly higher amounts of cell death are detected in layer V than in more superficial layers of older P9-11 mice (layer p<0.0001, post-hoc test sectors b and c < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of quantitative data.

claim: Spontaneous electrical activity is much more abundant and complex in S1 than in M1.
source: Interestingly, previous in vivo recordings of the developing neocortex demonstrated that spontaneous electricalactivity is much more abundant and complex in S1 (Yang et al., 2009; An et al., 2014) than in M1 (Yang et al., 2009; An et al., 2014; Khazipov et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous in vivo recording studies.

claim: S1 activity is characterized by a significantly higher spectral power in the delta to gamma range than M1 activity in urethane-anesthetized mice.
source: Comparative analysis of the in vivo network activity recorded in the two cortical areas demonstrates that S1 activity is characterized by a significantly higher spectral power in the delta to gamma range than M1 activity (Figure 4D1 and D2 and Figure 4—source data 1; two-way ANOVA, cortical area p<0.0001; frequency p<0.0001; n = 5 animals).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo electrophysiological recordings and spectral analysis shown in Figure 4D with statistical testing.

claim: In S1, the overall number of troughs (156 ± 27.8 min−1) is significantly higher than in M1 (63 ± 20 min−1) in urethane-anesthetized mice.
source: A detailed analysis of this activity further reveals that in S1, the overall number of troughs (Figure 4D3 and Figure 4—source data 1; 156 ± 27.8 min−1, n = 5 animals) and the median trough frequency (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; 1.43 Hz, n = 2333 events) is significantly higher than the overall number of troughs (63 ± 20 min−1; Mann Whitney test, p=0.0317) and median trough frequency (0.82 Hz; n = 944 events; Mann Whitney test, p<0.001) in M1.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of in vivo recordings shown in Figure 4D3 with statistical testing.

claim: In non-anesthetized animals, the spectral power of S1 in vivo activity is significantly higher than the spectral power of M1 in vivo activity.
source: Also under this condition, the spectral power of S1 in vivo activity is significantly higher than the spectral power of M1 in vivo activity (Figure 4E1 and E2 and Figure 4—source data 2; two-way ANOVA, cortical area p=0.0015, n = 5 animals).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo recordings in non-anesthetized animals shown in Figure 4E with statistical analysis.

claim: In non-anesthetized animals, the trough rate in S1 (159.7 ± 23.6 min−1) is significantly higher than the trough rate in M1 (51.9 ± 23.4 min−1).
source: Furthermore, the trough rate in S1 (Figure 4E3 and Figure 4—source data 2; 159.7 ± 23.6 min−1) is significantly higher than the trough rate in M1 (51.9 ± 23.4 min−1; Mann Whitney test p=0.03).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of in vivo recordings in non-anesthetized animals shown in Figure 4E3 with statistical testing.

claim: In vitro slices display a pattern of neuronal apoptosis similar to the in vivo situation with a high cell death density in cortical layers I-IV in M1 and significantly sparser aCasp3-positive neurons in the more lateral S1 sectors.
source: Subsequent immunhistochemical analysis revealed that these in vitro slices display a pattern of neuronal apoptosis similar to the in vivo situation – that is with a high cell death density in cortical layers I-IV in M1 and significantly sparser aCasp3-positive neurons in the more lateral S1 sectors (Figure 5A2 and A3; one-way ANOVA, R²=0.34, p<0.0001, n = 7 hemispheres from seven animals).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical analysis of in vitro slices shown in Figure 5A with statistical analysis.

claim: The overall rate of cell death in vitro is increased by about 4-fold compared to the in vivo situation.
source: But in comparison to the in vivo situation, the overall rate of cell death is increased by about 4-fold (in vivo: 34.39 ± 14.44 aCasp3/mm²; in vitro: 132.67 + 39.2 aCasp3/mm², t-test = 0.040).
evidence: This is supported by comparative quantitative analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Bath application of 4-AP/0 Mg2+ ACSF results in significantly lower numbers of apoptotic neurons compared to untreated slices.
source: Subsequent analysis of these slices shows significantly lower numbers of apoptotic neurons compared to untreated slices (Figure 5A3 and Figure 5—source data 1; two-way ANOVA, sector p<0.0001, electrical activity p<0.0001, n = 6 slices from six animals).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A3 with statistical analysis.

claim: At 3 hr following dissection, rates of apoptosis are already decreased in slices exposed to 4-AP/0 Mg2+ for two hours compared to control conditions.
source: At this earlier time point, rates of apoptosis are already decreased in slices exposed to 4-AP/0 Mg2+ for two hours compared to control conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; two-way ANOVA, sector p=0.001, electrical activity p=0.02).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B with statistical analysis.

claim: Disinhibition-induced activity by perfusing slices with 3 µM gabazine in low Mg2+ conditions results in a strong reduction in the rate of apoptosis in comparison to untreated control slices.
source: The elevated levels of activity induced by this second pharmacological model likewise result in a strong reduction in the rate of apoptosis in comparison to untreated control slices (Figure 5B and Figure 5—source data 2; two-way ANOVA, sector p=0.009, electrical activity p=0.001, n = 6 untreated hemispheres from six animals).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B with statistical analysis.

claim: The density of apoptotic cells in adult (P27) cortical neurons is very low in comparison to P5-7 mice.
source: Additional control experiments to investigate whether these effects are restricted to early developmental stages demonstrate that the density of apoptotic cells in adult (P27) cortical neurons is very low in comparison to P5-7 mice (Figure 5A3 and Figure 5—source data 1; two-way ANOVA, age p<0.0001, n = 6 hemispheres from three animals)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A3 with statistical analysis.

claim: In adult cortical slices, apoptotic cells are homogenously distributed throughout all cortical areas analyzed.
source: and homogenously distributed throughout all cortical areas analyzed (sectors p=0.30).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of adult cortical slice data.

claim: Interictal and ictal-like activity induced by 4-AP/0 Mg2+ treatment is not correlated to enhanced apoptotic rates in adult slices.
source: Interictal and ictal-like activity induced by 4-AP/0 Mg2+ treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, n = 6 hemispheres from three animals) is not correlated to enhanced apoptotic rates in these slices (electrical activity p=0.27).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Organotypic neocortical slices cultivated from newborn mice typically display spontaneous recurrent waves of activity propagating over the whole cortex.
source: Organotypic neocortical slices cultivated from newborn mice typically display spontaneous recurrent waves of activity propagating over the whole cortex (Conhaim et al., 2011; Heck et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Quantification of aCasp3-positive neurons in organotypic slices after 4 days in vitro does not reveal any significant difference in the rate of apoptosis between cortical sectors covering M1 and S1.
source: In line with our hypothesis, quantification of aCasp3-positive neurons in layers I to IV after 4 days in vitro (corresponding to P5-7) does not reveal any significant difference in the rate of apoptosis between cortical sectors covering M1 and S1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2; one-way ANOVA, sector p=0.74, R²=0.07, n = 7 slices from seven animals).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of organotypic cultures shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 with statistical analysis.

claim: Upon silencing of electrical network by 1 µM TTX in organotypic slices, the overall rate of apoptosis significantly increases.
source: Upon silencing of electrical network by 1 µM TTX, the overall rate of apoptosis significantly increases (Figure 5—figure supplement 2; two-way ANOVA, condition p=0.0001, n = 3 slices from three animals)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 with statistical analysis.

claim: Replay of in vivo activity in layers V-VI of the motor cortex results in a significant reduction of aCasp3-expressing neurons in the stimulated hemisphere when compared to the unstimulated, contralateral hemisphere.
source: As expected from our previous results, replay of in vivo activity in layers V-VI of the motor cortex results in a significant reduction of aCasp3-expressing neurons in the stimulated hemisphere when compared to the unstimulated, contralateral hemisphere (Figure 6C and Figure 6—source data 1; two-way ANOVA, sector p<0.0001, electrical activity p=0.0008, n = 6 slices from six animals).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C with statistical analysis.

claim: Replay of S1 activity has a significantly higher pro-survival effect than replayed M1 activity.
source: In line with our hypothesis, replay of S1 activity has a significantly higher pro-survival effect than replayed M1 activity (Figure 6D and Figure 6—source data 2; two-way ANOVA, stimulation pattern p=0.03, area p=0.63).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D with statistical analysis.

claim: A single intraperitoneal injection of kainate (2 mg/kg) induces tonic seizures in P5-7 mice within about 40 min.
source: Consistent with previous work in P6 rats (Puskarjov et al., 2015), a single intraperitoneal injection of kainate (2 mg/kg) induces tonic seizures in P5-7 mice within about 40 min.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and a citation to previous work.

claim: Modifying electrical activity levels in vivo affects the susceptibility of immature neurons to undergo apoptosis.
source: Quantification of apoptosis in M1 and S1 regions of kainate- versus saline-injected mice demonstrates that also in vivo, modifying electrical activity levels affects the susceptibility of immature neurons to undergo apoptosis (Figure 7A and Figure 7—source data 1; two-way ANOVA, sector p<0.0001, condition p=0.005).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A with statistical analysis.

claim: In the somatosensory cortex, rates of apoptosis are not significantly reduced upon induction of epileptiform activity by kainate.
source: Whereas in the somatosensory cortex, rates of apoptosis are not significantly reduced upon induction of epileptiform activity (control: 14.09 ± 2.49 aCasp3 positive cells/mm², n = 7 mice; kainate: 9.28 ± 1.57 aCasp3 positive cells/mm², n = 9 mice, post-hoc test p>0.05)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Levels of apoptosis in the primary motor cortex are significantly lower in kainate-injected mice (30.25 ± 6.16 aCasp3 positive cells/mm²) than in saline-injected mice (52.03 ± 6.00 aCasp3 positive cells/mm²).
source: levels of apoptosis in the primary motor cortex are significantly lower in kainate-injected mice (30.25 ± 6.16 aCasp3 positive cells/mm²) than in saline-injected mice (52.03 ± 6.00 aCasp3 positive cells/mm², post-hoc test p<0.01).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis with statistical testing.

claim: A substantial portion of electrical activity in S1 is generated in the sensory periphery.
source: A substantial portion of electrical activity in S1 is generated in the sensory periphery (Yang et al., 2009; Minlebaev et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Whisker deafferentation leads to an increased density of apoptotic neurons in the corresponding contralateral barrel field (18.74 ± 1.88 aCasp3 positive cells/mm²) as compared to the somatosensory cortex of the ipsilateral hemisphere receiving non-obstructed whisker afferents (13.77 ± 1.41 aCasp3 positive cells/mm²).
source: Quantification of aCasp3-labeled cells shows that already within 5 hr, whisker deafferentation leads to an increased density of apoptotic neurons in the corresponding contralateral barrel field (Figure 7B and Figure 7—source data 2; 18.74 ± 1.88 aCasp3 positive cells/mm², n = 10 mice) as compared to the somatosensory cortex of the ipsilateral hemisphere receiving non-obstructed whisker afferents (13.77 ± 1.41 aCasp3 positive cells/mm²; t-test, p=0.038).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B with statistical analysis.

claim: Electrical activity regulates cell death in the developing cortex in a cortical area-dependent manner.
source: In summary, our data show for the first time that electrical activity regulates cell death in the developing cortex in a cortical area-dependent manner and thus represents an important factor for the functional and structural maturation of the brain.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: A mediolateral apoptosis profile of neocortical neurons comparable to the M1 versus S1 difference has been shown previously.
source: While a mediolateral apoptosis profile of neocortical neurons comparable to the M1 versus S1 difference reported in the present study has been shown previously (Ikonomidou et al., 1999; Verney et al., 2000; Mosley et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A direct relation of apoptotic densities to functional neocortical areas has not been reported before this study.
source: a direct relation of apoptotic densities to functional neocortical areas has, to our knowledge, not been reported before.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current study's findings.

claim: Neocortical slices reveal a higher number of apoptotic neurons compared to the same neocortical areas in vivo, possibly due to the lower rate of spontaneous electrical activity in acute slice preparations.
source: Interestingly, neocortical slices reveal a higher number of apoptotic neurons compared to the same neocortical areas in vivo. This observation could be due to the lower rate of spontaneous electrical activity in acute slice preparations.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed data and the hypothesis of the study.

claim: The effect of kainate on reducing apoptosis is only significant for M1, but not for S1, either because the smaller number of apoptotic neurons in S1 impedes the analysis or because differences in electrical activity between S1 and M1 influence the amount of additional spikes introduced by convulsive conditions.
source: This effect is only significant for M1, but not for S1, either because the smaller number of apoptotic neurons in S1 impedes the analysis of such rescue experiments, or because differences in the electrical activity between S1 and M1 influence the amount of additional spikes introduced by convulsive conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: The survival of cortical neurons in silenced organotypic cultures is not due to an alternative pro-survival pathway but rather to the presence of pro-survival factors present within the culture medium.
source: We therefore hypothesize that the survival of cortical neurons in silenced organotypic cultures is not due to an alternative pro-survival pathway but rather to the presence of pro-survival factors present within the culture medium.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain their observations.

claim: Layers II to IV show more apoptotic neurons than layers V and VI in the first postnatal week.
source: This finding is in line with a previous report demonstrating that layers II to IV show more apoptotic neurons than layers V and VI in the first postnatal week (Heumann and Leuba, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In vivo recordings in the M1 region of P6 mice across all neocortical layers do not show a negative correlation between activity levels and rates of apoptosis.
source: Surprisingly, in vivo recordings in the M1 region of P6 mice across all neocortical layers do not show a negative correlation between activity levels and rates of apoptosis (unpublished data).
evidence: This is based on unpublished data from the authors.

claim: Lower layer VI contains the early-generated subplate neurons.
source: Lower layer VI contains the early-generated subplate neurons (Hoerder-Suabedissen and Molnár, 2013; Kanold and Luhmann, 2010; Higashi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A proportion of subplate neurons is eliminated by apoptosis during the first postnatal weeks.
source: It has been suggested that a proportion of these neurons is eliminated by apoptosis during the first postnatal weeks (Price et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The low cell death density in layer VI is attributed to the subplate layer being very thin (about 50 µm-width) and apoptotic neurons being cleared away by macrophages within 2.5 hr.
source: We attribute this low cell death density to two reasons. First, the subplate layer represents a very thin layer of about 50 µm-width located between the white matter and layer VI-a (Hoerder-Suabedissen and Molnár, 2013). Because, apoptotic neurons are cleared away by macrophages with 2.5 hr (Thomaidou et al., 1997), the chance to stain apoptotic neurons in this layer is very low.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on anatomical knowledge and a citation about macrophage clearance.

claim: Only a fraction of subplate neurons is eliminated by apoptosis, while other subplate neurons such as Nurr1 or Lpar1-GFP-labeled neurons survive beyond the postnatal period.
source: Second, recent reports have demonstrated that only a fraction of subplate neurons is eliminated by apoptosis, while other subplate neurons such as Nurr1 or Lpar1-GFP-labeled neurons survive beyond the postnatal period (Hoerder-Suabedissen and Molnár, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The layer VI-b consists of persistent neurons from the subplate layer.
source: In line with the existence of a substantial fraction of surviving subplate neurons, it has been recently shown that the layer VI-b consists of persistent neurons from the subplate layer (Marx et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: In the immature brain, including that of humans, a variety of intrinsically-generated and sensory-evoked activity patterns can be observed in different cortical areas.
source: In the immature brain, including that of humans, a variety of intrinsically-generated and sensory-evoked activity patterns can be observed in different cortical areas (An et al., 2014; Milh et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2009; Khazipov et al., 2004; Khazipov and Luhmann, 2006; Kilb et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The distinct levels of spontaneous neuronal activity in the immature sensory, motor or association cortex have been frequently attributed to the development of adequate connectivity.
source: The distinct levels of spontaneous neuronal activity in the immature sensory, motor or association cortex have been frequently attributed to the development of adequate connectivity (Chen and Ghosh, 2005; Luhmann et al., 2016; Spitzer, 2012; Hartung et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Human brains display activity patterns similar to the rodent ones.
source: Human brains display activity patterns similar to the rodent ones (Khazipov and Luhmann, 2006; Vanhatalo and Kaila, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The electroencephalogram of preterm babies exhibits at an equivalent developmental period a local rhythmic activity in a similar frequency range than spindle bursts: the so-called delta brushes.
source: For instance the electroencephalogram of preterm babies exhibits at an equivalent developmental period a local rhythmic activity in a similar frequency range than spindle bursts: the so-called delta brushes (Milh et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Subsequent modification of the number of cortical neurons results in pathophysiological outcomes such as autistic-like behavior.
source: As revealed by previous animal studies, subsequent modification of the number of cortical neurons results in pathophysiological outcomes such as autistic-like behavior (Fang et al., 2014; Nakamura et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous animal studies.

claim: A large fraction of children suffering from autistic spectrum disorders shows an elevated number of neocortical neurons.
source: In line with behavioral deficits as a consequence of changes in the neuronal population size, a large fraction of children suffering from autistic spectrum disorders shows an elevated number of neocortical neurons (Courchesne et al., 2011; Casanova et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It has been proposed that mostly enhanced neurogenesis causes autism-related increase in cerebral volume.
source: While it has been proposed that mostly enhanced neurogenesis causes this autism-related increase in cerebral volume (Kaushik and Zarbalis, 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Activity-dependent alterations in apoptosis must be considered as a possible cause of autism-related increase in cerebral volume.
source: we propose that activity-dependent alterations in apoptosis must be also considered as possible cause.
evidence: This is a proposal by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Sensory whisker deprivation during the first postnatal days induces not only deficits in tactile sensation but also exacerbated fear and anxiety-related responses as well as impaired social behavior.
source: Further, a recent study reported that sensory whisker deprivation during the first postnatal days, that is through the period covering the critical period of cell death, induces not only the expected deficits in tactile sensation but also exacerbated fear and anxiety-related responses as well as impaired social behavior (Soumiya et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Neuronal electrical activity at pre- and peri-natal stages, besides affecting neuronal proliferation, migration or integration, also directly influences apoptosis.
source: In conclusion we demonstrate that neuronal electrical activity at pre- and peri-natal stages, besides affecting neuronal proliferation, migration or integration (De Marco García et al., 2015, 2011; Weissman et al., 2004; López-Bendito and Molnár, 2003), also directly influences apoptosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings and citations to previous work on other effects of neuronal activity.

claim: Physiological activity patterns are essential for the establishment and refinement of functional circuits in the cortex.
source: This implies on the one hand that physiological activity patterns are essential for the establishment and refinement of functional circuits in the cortex
evidence: This is an implication drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Drugs or pathophysiological conditions interfering with early activity and cell death likely contribute to many neuropsychiatric diseases.
source: and that drugs or pathophysiological conditions interfering with early activity and cell death likely contribute to many neuropsychiatric diseases (Brown et al., 2005; van Diessen et al., 2015; Ben-Ari, 2015; Silva et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an implication supported by citations to previous studies on neuropsychiatric diseases.

claim: aCasp3 is an early marker of irreversible entry in the apoptosis process.
source: For that purpose, apoptotic cells were labeled with an antibody against activated-Caspase3 (aCasp3), an early marker of irreversible entry in the apoptosis process (Jänicke et al., 1998)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: TUNEL staining labels fragmented nuclei when cell death process is fully executed.
source: The spatial pattern of cell death at P5-7 detected by aCasp3 immunohistochemistry was confirmed by TUNEL staining, which labels fragmented nuclei when cell death process is fully executed (Gavrieli et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation describing the TUNEL method.

claim: aCasp3 is a reliable marker to identify apoptotic neurons.
source: validating aCasp3 as a reliable marker to identify apoptotic neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison between aCasp3 and TUNEL staining results.

claim: The spatial pattern of apoptosis in the cortex cannot be explained by a different maturation state in M1 versus S1.
source: The spatial pattern of apoptosis in the cortex cannot be explained by a different maturation state in M1 versus S1 (Verney et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The spatial pattern of apoptosis is more likely caused by either area-dependent differences in neuron-intrinsic properties or by area-specific pro-apoptotic versus pro-survival signals.
source: but is more likely caused by either area-dependent differences in neuron-intrinsic properties or by area-specific pro-apoptotic versus pro-survival signals.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations.

claim: Previous in vitro studies have demonstrated that electrical activity promotes neuronal survival during early development.
source: Previous in vitro studies have demonstrated that electrical activity promotes neuronal survival during early development (Murase et al., 2011; Golbs et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous in vitro studies.

claim: Electrical activity functions as a pro-survival factor.
source: indicating that electrical activity functions as a pro-survival factor.
evidence: This is an inference based on previous studies and the current findings.

claim: Both cortical regions (M1 and S1) display intermittent network oscillatory activity.
source: As previously reported for early neocortical networks in vivo (Yang et al., 2009; An et al., 2014; Khazipov et al., 2004), both cortical regions display intermittent network oscillatory activity (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo recordings shown in Figure 4C and citations to previous studies.

claim: The area-dependent level of activity is not due to a differential effect of urethane between M1 and S1.
source: To verify that the area-dependent level of activity is not due to a differential effect of urethane between M1 and S1, we next recorded the activity in the upper layers of S1 and M1 in non-anesthetized animals.
evidence: This is addressed by performing recordings in non-anesthetized animals.

claim: In vitro slice preparations allow a better control of electrical activity.
source: In order to address the question whether differences in electrical activity between M1 and S1 are causally related to the different rates of apoptosis between these two cortical areas, we next used in vitro slice preparations that allow a better control of electrical activity.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about experimental methods.

claim: Increasing spontaneous activity for two hours is sufficient to significantly lower the amount of neurons undergoing cell death in the immature cortex.
source: These data indicate that in vitro, increasing spontaneous activity for two hours are sufficient to significantly lower the amount of neurons undergoing cell death in the immature cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from pharmacological treatments.

claim: Both the high occurrence of neuronal apoptosis and the pro-survival effect of increased activity are hallmark features of immature cortical networks.
source: These results demonstrate that both the high occurrence of neuronal apoptosis and the pro-survival effect of increased activity are hallmark features of immature cortical networks.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison between immature and adult cortical slices.

claim: Regional differences in rates of apoptosis are abolished in organotypic cultures in the presence of equivalent spontaneous electrical activity levels.
source: Hence, regional differences in rates of apoptosis are abolished in the presence of equivalent spontaneous electrical activity levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the organotypic culture experiments.

claim: An activity-dependent process underlies the regional differences in apoptosis.
source: demonstrating that an activity-dependent process underlies these observations.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the TTX experiments in organotypic cultures.

claim: Elevated electrical activity exerts a strong pro-survival signal on immature cortical neurons during the critical period of cell death and diminishes the area-specific profile of apoptosis.
source: In conclusion, these results demonstrate that elevated electrical activity exerts a strong pro-survival signal on immature cortical neurons during the critical period of cell death and diminishes the area-specific profile of apoptosis
evidence: This is a conclusion based on all the in vitro experiments.

claim: The spatial pattern of apoptosis does not rely only on the area identity of cortical neurons.
source: indicating that the spatial pattern does not rely only on the area identity of cortical neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: The replay pattern of M1 activity consisted of 24 ± 3.1 electrical stimuli/min and the replay pattern of S1 activity had a significantly higher rate of 125 ± 15.2 stimuli/min.
source: The replay pattern of M1 activity consisted of 24 ± 3.1 electrical stimuli/min (n = 2 stimulus protocols) and the replay pattern of S1 activity had a significantly higher rate of 125 ± 15.2 stimuli/min (n = 2 stimulus protocols).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for the replay experiments.

claim: Both stimulation protocols and the resulting activity resembled the temporal distribution of events in vivo.
source: Both stimulation protocols and the resulting activity resembled the temporal distribution of events in vivo (Figure 6A2 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of in vitro and in vivo activity patterns shown in Figure 6A2 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Different activity levels in M1 and S1 can be causal for the observed differences in area-specific rates of apoptosis.
source: In summary, these results provide evidence that the different activity levels in M1 and S1 can be causal for the observed differences in area-specific rates of apoptosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the replay experiments.

claim: High levels of activity significantly lower the incidence of neuronal apoptosis in vivo, especially in a cortical area that encounters physiologically low levels of electrical activity.
source: This result demonstrates that also in vivo, high levels of activity significantly lower the incidence of neuronal apoptosis, especially in a cortical area that encounters physiologically low levels of electrical activity, further supporting our hypothesis that neuronal activity controls the area-specific pattern of apoptosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the kainate injection experiments.

claim: Periphery-driven electrical activity in S1 provides an anti-apoptotic signal that contributes to the area-specific differences in rates of apoptosis.
source: These results provide direct evidence that periphery-driven electrical activity in S1 provides an anti-apoptotic signal that contributes to the area-specific differences in rates of apoptosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the whisker deafferentation experiments.

claim: Electrical activity represents an important factor for the functional and structural maturation of the brain.
source: In summary, our data show for the first time that electrical activity regulates cell death in the developing cortex in a cortical area-dependent manner and thus represents an important factor for the functional and structural maturation of the brain.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental findings.

claim: Apoptosis and early spontaneous synchronous activity are phylogenetically conserved hallmark features of immature cortical networks.
source: While size, complexity and processing capacity of the cerebral cortex have incredibly expanded during mammalian evolution, apoptosis (Oppenheim, 1991) and early spontaneous synchronous activity (Khazipov and Luhmann, 2006), two temporally overlapping hallmark features of immature cortical networks, are phylogenetically conserved.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Electrical activity and programmed cell death are essential elements which mutually interact to ensure the proper development of the cortex.
source: It is therefore reasonable to hypothesize that both processes - electrical activity and programmed cell death - are essential elements which might not only co-occur, but mutually interact to ensure the proper development of the cortex.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Neuronal activity is a major determinant of the region-dependent rate of apoptosis in the developing neocortex.
source: We conclude from these results that neuronal activity is a major determinant of the region-dependent rate of apoptosis in the developing neocortex.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all experimental findings.

claim: The immature cortex displays higher rates of apoptosis than the adult cortex.
source: In accordance with previous reports (Ferrer et al., 1994; Southwell et al., 2012; Nikolić et al., 2013), the present study shows that the immature cortex displays higher rates of apoptosis than the adult cortex.
evidence: This is supported by the current study's data and citations to previous reports.

claim: During the first postnatal week, functionally diverse neocortical areas reveal distinct levels of neuronal apoptosis.
source: We additionally demonstrate that during the first postnatal week, functionally diverse neocortical areas reveal distinct levels of neuronal apoptosis.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study.

claim: Apoptosis is an important process for the establishment of functionally distinct neural circuits during early development.
source: and thus underline the important role of apoptosis for the establishment of functionally distinct neural circuits during early development (Ferrer et al., 1994; Southwell et al., 2012; Nikolić et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The rate of neuronal apoptosis at early developmental stages is to a large extent negatively regulated by electrical/synaptic activity in vitro.
source: It has been demonstrated in vitro that the rate of neuronal apoptosis at early developmental stages is to a large extent negatively regulated by electrical/synaptic activity (Golbs et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous in vitro study.

claim: An elevation of neuronal activity by pro-convulsive conditions diminishes the rates of apoptosis in the immature neocortex under in vitro and in vivo conditions.
source: In line with these in vitro results, the present study confirms that an elevation of neuronal activity by pro-convulsive conditions diminishes the rates of apoptosis in the immature neocortex under in vitro and in vivo conditions.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study.

claim: Already two hours of elevated electrical activity are sufficient to significantly decrease the number of apoptotic cortical neurons.
source: We further show that already two hours of elevated electrical activity are sufficient to significantly decrease the number of apoptotic cortical neurons.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study.

claim: Immature brains are highly susceptible to acute changes in electrical activity.
source: As immature brains are highly susceptible to acute changes in electrical activity (Ben-Ari and Holmes, 2006), this stresses the clinical relevance of the presented data.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Regional differences in electrical activity are indeed causal for the different levels of apoptosis in functionally distinct neocortical areas.
source: In summary, these results indicate that electrical activity and levels of apoptosis are negatively correlated and provide strong evidence that regional differences in electrical activity are indeed causal for the different levels of apoptosis in functionally distinct neocortical areas.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the replay and sensory deprivation experiments.

claim: Organotypic slices, in which the electrical activity is synchronized over the whole preparation, do not display any regional differences in apoptotic rates.
source: One additional intriguing observation of the present study is that organotypic slices, in which the electrical activity is synchronized over the whole preparation, do not display any regional differences in apoptotic rates.
evidence: This is a finding from the organotypic culture experiments.

claim: Electrical activity per se provides the major regionalization cue regulating specific rates of apoptosis.
source: Since in this preparation blockade of all electrical activity with TTX also does not uncover regional differences, it is tempting to postulate that electrical activity per se provide the major regionalization cue regulating specific rates of apoptosis.
evidence: This is a postulation based on the organotypic culture experiments.

claim: The effect of elevated neuronal activity dramatically reduces the number of neurons undergoing apoptosis already after 4 hr.
source: While the effect of elevated neuronal activity dramatically reduces the number of neurons undergoing apoptosis already after 4 hr, the effect of chronic activity blockade seems to be more moderate.
evidence: This is based on the experimental observations.

claim: In vivo, the absence of synaptic transmission leads to a dramatic apoptotic response directly after neurons have assembled.
source: In vivo, the absence of synaptic transmission leads to a dramatic apoptotic response directly after neurons have assembled (Verhage et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: A direct influence of sensory-driven and spontaneous neuronal activity on the size and probably also the composition of the cellular pool underlying neuronal networks must be considered as an important element during brain formation.
source: The results of the present study demonstrate that a direct influence of sensory-driven and spontaneous neuronal activity on the size and probably also the composition of the cellular pool underlying neuronal networks must also be considered as an important element during brain formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: Human preterm activity patterns most probably also modulate neuronal apoptosis in the developing human brain.
source: These human preterm activity patterns most probably also modulate neuronal apoptosis in the developing human brain
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity between human and rodent activity patterns.

claim: Inadequate activity can lead to persistent changes in the nervous system through modulation of neuronal apoptosis.
source: which points to an additional mechanism by which inadequate activity can lead to persistent changes in the nervous system.
evidence: This is an implication of the study's findings.
